vsm2.18:1.1:
Now, it was said earlier (XIV.32) that he “should first fortify his knowledge by learning and questioning
about those things that are the ‘soil’
vsm2.18:1.2: after he has perfected the two purifications—purification of virtue and purification of consciousness—that are the ‘roots.’”
vsm2.18:1.3: Now, of those, purification of virtue is the quite purified fourfold virtue beginning with Pātimokkha restraint;
vsm2.18:1.4: and that has already been dealt with in detail in the Description of Virtue; (Chs. I and II)
vsm2.18:1.5: and the purification of consciousness, namely, the eight attainments together with access concentration,
vsm2.18:1.6:
has also been dealt with in detail in all its aspects in the Description of Concentration, (Chs.
III to XIII) stated under the heading of “consciousness” in the introductory verse.
vsm2.18:1.7: So those two purifications should be understood in detail as given there.
vsm2.18:2.1:
But it was said above (XIV.32) that “The five purifications, purification of view, purification by overcoming doubt,
purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path,
vsm2.18:2.2: purification by knowledge and vision of the way, and purification by knowledge and vision, are the ‘trunk.’”
vsm2.18:2.3: Herein, “purification of view” is the correct seeing of mentality-materiality.
vsm2.18:3.1:
(1) DEFINITION BASED ON THE FOUR PRIMARIES
(a) Starting with Mentality

One who wants to accomplish this, if, firstly, his vehicle is serenity, should emerge from any
fine-material or immaterial jhāna, except the base consisting of neither perception nor non-perception,
vsm2.18:3.2:
and he should discern, according to characteristic, function, etc., the jhāna factors consisting of applied thought,
etc., and the states associated with them, that is, feeling, perception, and so on.
vsm2.18:3.3:
When he has done so, all that should be defined as “mentality” (nāma) in the sense of bending
(namana) because of its bending on to the object.
vsm2.18:4.1: Then, just as a man, by following a snake that he has seen in his house, finds its abode,
vsm2.18:4.2: so too this meditator scrutinizes that mentality, he seeks to find out what its occurrence is supported by
vsm2.18:4.3: and he sees that it is supported by the matter of the heart.
vsm2.18:4.4: After that, he discerns as materiality the primary elements, which are the heart’s support,
vsm2.18:4.5: and the remaining, derived kinds of materiality that have the elements as their support.
vsm2.18:4.6: He defines all that as “materiality” (rūpa) because it is “molested” (ruppana) by cold, etc..
vsm2.18:4.7: After that he defines in brief as “mentality-materiality” (nāma-rūpa) the mentality that has the characteristic of “bending”
vsm2.18:4.8: and the materiality that has the characteristic of “being molested.”
vsm2.18:5.1:
(b) Starting with Materiality

But one whose vehicle is pure insight, or that same aforesaid one whose vehicle is serenity,
vsm2.18:5.2:
discerns the four elements in brief or in detail in one of the various ways
given in the chapter on the definition of the four elements (XI.27ff.).
vsm2.18:5.3:
Then, when the elements have become clear in their correct essential characteristics,
firstly, in the case of head hair originated by kamma there become plain ten instances of materiality
vsm2.18:5.4: (rūpāni) with the body decad thus: the four elements, colour, odour, flavour, nutritive essence, and life, and body sensitivity.
vsm2.18:5.5: And because the sex decad is present there too there are another ten that is, the same nine with sex instead of body sensitivity.
vsm2.18:5.6:
And since the octad-with-nutritive-essence-as-eighth that is, the four elements and colour, odour,
flavour, and nutritive essence, originated by nutriment, and that originated by temperature,
and that originated by consciousness are present there too, there are another twenty-four.
vsm2.18:5.7:
So there is a total of forty-four instances of materiality in the case of each of the twenty-four
bodily parts of fourfold origination.
vsm2.18:5.8:
But in the case of the four, namely, sweat, tears, spittle, and snot, which are originated by temperature and by consciousness,
there are sixteen instances of materiality with the two octads-with-nutritive-essence-as-eighth in each.
vsm2.18:5.9:
In the case of the four, namely, gorge, dung, pus, and urine, which are originated by temperature, eight instances of materiality
become plain in each with the octad-with-nutritive-essence-as-eighth in what is originated only by temperature.
vsm2.18:5.10: This, in the first place, is the method in the case of the thirty-two bodily aspects.
vsm2.18:6.1: But there are ten more aspects that become clear when those thirty-two aspects have become clear.
vsm2.18:6.2:
And as regards these, firstly, nine instances of materiality, that is, the octad-with-nutritive-essence-as-eighth plus life,
become plain in the case of the kamma-born part of heat (fire) that digests what is eaten, etc.,
vsm2.18:6.3:
and likewise nine instances of materiality, that is, the octad-with-nutritive-essence-as-eighth plus
sound, in the case of the consciousness-born part of air consisting of in-breaths and out-breaths;
vsm2.18:6.4:
and thirty-three instances of materiality, that is, the kamma-born life-ennead and the three
octads-with-nutritive-essence-as-eighth in the case of each of the remaining eight parts that are of fourfold origination.
vsm2.18:7.1:
And when these instances of materiality derived by clinging from the primaries have thus become plain in detail in the case
of these forty-two aspects, that is, thirty-two parts of the body, four modes of fire, and six modes of air,
vsm2.18:7.2:
another sixty instances of materiality become plain with the physical heart- basis and the five sense doors,
that is, with the heart-basis decad and the five decads beginning with the eye decad.
vsm2.18:7.3: Taking all these together under the characteristic of “being molested,” he sees them as “materiality.”
vsm2.18:8.1: When he has discerned materiality thus, the immaterial states become plain to him in accordance with the sense doors,
vsm2.18:8.2:
that is to say, the eighty-one kinds of mundane consciousness consisting of the two sets of five consciousnesses ((34)–(38)
and (50)–(54)), the three kinds of mind element ((39), (55) and (70)) and the sixty-eight kinds of mind-consciousness element;
vsm2.18:8.3:
and then seven consciousness-concomitants, that is, (i) contact, feeling, perception, (ii) volition, (vii) life,
(viii) steadiness of consciousness, and (xxx) attention, which are invariably conascent with all these consciousnesses.
vsm2.18:8.4:
The supramundane kinds of consciousness, however, are not discernible either by one who is practicing
pure insight or by one whose vehicle is serenity because they are out of their reach.
vsm2.18:8.5: Taking all these immaterial states together under the characteristic of “bending,” he sees them as “mentality.”
vsm2.18:8.6: This is how one meditator defines mentality-materiality in detail through the method of defining the four elements.
vsm2.18:9.1:
(2) DEFINITION BASED ON THE EIGHTEEN ELEMENTS

Another does it by means of the eighteen elements. How?
vsm2.18:9.2: Here a bhikkhu considers the elements thus: “There are in this person the eye element, … the mind-consciousness element.”
vsm2.18:9.3:
Instead of taking the piece of flesh variegated with white and black circles, having
length and breath, and fastened in the eye socket with a string of sinew, which the world terms “an eye,”
vsm2.18:9.4:
he defines as “eye element” the eye sensitivity of the kind described among the kinds of derived
materiality in the Description of the Aggregates (XIV.47).
vsm2.18:10.1:
But he does not define as “eye element” the remaining instances of materiality, which total fifty-three,
that is, the nine conascent instances of materiality consisting of the four primary elements, which are its support,
vsm2.18:10.2:
the four concomitant instances of materiality, namely, colour, odour,
flavour, and nutritive essence, and the sustaining life faculty;
vsm2.18:10.3: and also the twenty kamma-born instances of materiality that are there too, consisting of the body decad and sex decad;
vsm2.18:10.4:
and the twenty-four unclung-to instances of materiality consisting of the three
octads-with-nutritive-essence-as-eighth, which are originated by nutriment and so on.
vsm2.18:10.5: The same method applies to the ear element and the rest.
vsm2.18:10.6: But in the case of the body element the remaining instances of materiality total forty-three,
vsm2.18:10.7: though some say forty-five by adding sound and making nine each for the temperature-born and consciousness-born sound.
vsm2.18:11.1:
So these five sensitivities, and their five respective objective fields, that is, visible data, sounds, odours,
flavours, and tangible data, make ten instances of materiality, which are ten of the eighteen elements.
vsm2.18:11.2: The remaining instances of materiality are the mental-data element only.
vsm2.18:11.3:
The consciousness that occurs with the eye as its support and contingent upon a visible datum
is called “eye-consciousness element” and likewise with the ear and so on.
vsm2.18:11.4: In this way the two sets of five consciousnesses are the five “consciousness elements.”
vsm2.18:11.5: The three kinds of consciousness consisting of mind element ((39), (55) and (70)) are the single “mind element.”
vsm2.18:11.6:
The sixty-eight kinds of mind-consciousness element are the “mind-consciousness element.”
So all the eighty-one kinds of mundane consciousness make up seven kinds of consciousness element;
vsm2.18:11.7: and the contact, etc., associated therewith are the mental-data element. So ten-and-a-half elements are materiality
vsm2.18:11.8:
and seven-and-a-half elements are mentality. This is how one meditator defines
mentality-materiality by means of the eighteen elements.
vsm2.18:12.1:
(3) DEFINITION BASED ON THE TWELVE BASES

Another does it by means of the twelve bases. How?
vsm2.18:12.2:
He defines as “eye base” the sensitivity only, leaving out the fifty-three remaining
instances of materiality, in the way described for the eye element.
vsm2.18:12.3:
And in the way described there he also defines the elements of the ear, nose,
tongue, and body, as “ear base, nose base, tongue base, body base.”
vsm2.18:12.4:
He defines five states that are their respective objective fields as “visible-data base,
sound base, odour base, flavour base, tangible-data base.”
vsm2.18:12.5: He defines the seven mundane consciousness elements as “mind base.”
vsm2.18:12.6: He defines the contact, etc., associated there with and also the remaining instances of materiality as “mental-data base.”
vsm2.18:12.7:
So here ten-and-a-half bases are materiality and one-and-a-half bases are mentality.
This is how one meditator defines mentality-materiality by means of the twelve bases.
vsm2.18:13.1:
(4) DEFINITION BASED ON THE FIVE AGGREGATES

Another defines it more briefly than that by means of the aggregates. How?
vsm2.18:13.2:
Here a bhikkhu defines as “the materiality aggregate” all the following twenty-seven instances of materiality,
that is, the seventeen instances of materiality consisting of the four primaries of fourfold
origination in this body and dependent colour, odour, flavour, and nutritive essence,
vsm2.18:13.4:
and then the ten instances of materiality, that is, bodily intimation, verbal intimation,
the space element, and the lightness, malleability, wieldiness, growth, continuity,
vsm2.18:13.5:
aging, and impermanence of materiality, which ten instances of materiality are, however, not suitable for comprehension since
they are merely the mode-alteration and the limitation-of-interval; they are not produced and are not concrete materiality,
vsm2.18:13.6:
but they are reckoned as materiality because they are mode-alterations,
and limitation-of-interval, of various instances of materiality.
vsm2.18:13.7: So he defines all these twenty-seven instances of materiality as the “the materiality aggregate.”
vsm2.18:13.8: He defines the feeling that arises together with the eighty-one kinds of mundane consciousness as the “feeling aggregate,”
vsm2.18:13.9:
the perception associated therewith as the “perception aggregate,” the formations associated therewith
as the “formations aggregate,” and the consciousness as the “consciousness aggregate.”
vsm2.18:13.10:
So by defining the materiality aggregate as “materiality” and the four immaterial aggregates
as “mentality,” he defines mentality-materiality by means of the five aggregates.
vsm2.18:14.1:
(5) BRIEF DEFINITION BASED ON THE FOUR PRIMARIES

Another discerns “materiality” in his person briefly thus: “Any kind of materiality whatever all consists of the four
primary elements and the materiality derived from the four primary elements” (M I 222),
vsm2.18:14.2: and he likewise discerns the mind base and a part of the mental data base as “mentality.”
vsm2.18:14.3: Then he defines mentality-materiality in brief thus: “This mentality and this materiality are called ‘mentality-materiality.’”
vsm2.18:15.1:
IF THE IMMATERIAL FAILS TO BECOME EVIDENT

But if he has discerned materiality in one of these ways, and while he is trying to discern
the immaterial it does not become evident to him owing to its subtlety,
vsm2.18:15.2: then he should not give up but should again and again comprehend, give attention to, discern, and define materiality only.
vsm2.18:16.1:
Just as, when a man with eyes looks for the reflection of his face in a dirty looking-glass and sees no reflection,
he does not throw the looking-glass away because the reflection does not appear;
vsm2.18:16.2: on the contrary, he polishes it again and again, and then the reflection becomes plain of itself when the looking-glass is clean—
vsm2.18:16.3:
and just as, when a man needing oil puts sesame flour in a basin and wets it with water and no oil
comes out with only one or two pressings, he does not throw the sesame flour away;
vsm2.18:16.4:
but on the contrary, he wets it again and again with hot water and squeezes and presses
it, and as he does so clear sesame oil comes out—
vsm2.18:16.5:
or just as, when a man wanting to clarify water has taken a katuka nut and put his hand inside the pot and rubbed
it once or twice but the water does not come clear, he does not throw the katuka nut away;
vsm2.18:16.6: on the contrary, he rubs it again and again, and as he does so the fine mud subsides and the water becomes transparent and clear—
vsm2.18:16.7:
so too, the bhikkhu should not give up, but he should again and again comprehend,
give attention to, discern and define materiality only.
vsm2.18:17.1:
For in proportion as materiality becomes quite definite, disentangled and quite clear to him, so the defilements
that are opposing him subside, his consciousness becomes clear like the water above the precipitated mud,
vsm2.18:17.2: and the immaterial states that have that materiality as their object become plain of themselves too.
vsm2.18:17.3:
And this meaning can also be explained in this way by other analogies such as the pressing of sugarcane, the beating
of criminals to make them confess, the taming of an ox, the churning of curds to produce butter, and the cooking of fish.
